title: Vacpack vs Groupon Getaway: Which One Is Actually Cheaper?
metaTitle: Vacpack vs Groupon Getaway: Which Is Cheaper | VacationDeals.to
metaDescription: Vacpack or Groupon getaway? See the honest price math, the strings attached to each, and which one wins for a cheap resort stay in 2026.
author: The VacationDeals.to Team
bluf: A vacpack is almost always the cheaper room, but it comes with a 90-120 minute timeshare presentation you have to sit through. A Groupon getaway is more relaxed with no tour, but you pay closer to real hotel prices. If you can handle the pitch, the vacpack wins on raw dollars becuase your paying $49-$199 for nights that would normally cost alot more.
heroImageAlt: Split image of a resort pool on one side and a phone showing a deal app on the other
content:
I spent a whole Tuesday night with two browser tabs open, a Groupon getaway in one and a $59 Westgate vacpack in the other, arguing with myself like a crazy person. My wife walked past, looked at the screen, and asked why I was treating a cheap weekend like a chess match. Honestly? Becuase the two deals looked similar on the surface and were completely different underneath.

Bottom Line Up Front: A vacpack is almost always the cheaper room, but it comes with a 90-120 minute timeshare presentation. A Groupon getaway skips the tour and stays relaxed, but you pay closer to real hotel rates. If you can sit the pitch, the vacpack wins on raw price becuase your paying $49-$199 for nights that would otherwise cost way more.

Is a vacpack cheaper than a Groupon getaway?

Yes, a vacpack is usually cheaper than a Groupon getaway, but only becuase you agree to attend a timeshare presentation to unlock the price. A vacpack runs $49-$199 for two to five nights at places like Orlando, Vegas, or Branson, while a comparable Groupon getaway often lands in the $200-$600 range for the same kind of stay. The gap is real, and its the presentation that pays for it.

Groupon getaways are basically discounted hotel bookings. There nice, they're flexible, and nobody makes you sit anywhere. But the discount comes off a normal room rate, so the floor is higher. A vacpack pushes the price way lower on purpose, because the resort is betting you'll fall in love with the place and buy points later.

Two cheap trips, two very different catches

What is the real catch with each one?

The catch with a vacpack is time and pressure: you and a partner sit a 90-120 minute sales tour, usually with an age and income requirement, and you have to say no a bunch of times. The catch with a Groupon is fine print: blackout dates, resort fees tacked on at check-in, and deals that quietly expire. Neither one is a scam, they just hide the cost in different places.

Me and my wife have done both. The Groupon felt easier in the moment, but we paid for that ease. The vacpack felt like work for two hours, and then we had four days that cost less than one night back home. You're basically choosing what you'd rather spend: money or a morning.

FactorVacpackGroupon Getaway
Typical price$49-$199 for 2-5 nights$200-$600 for a similar stay
The catch90-120 min timeshare tourBlackout dates, resort fees
Who qualifiesUsually 25+, ~$50K income, couplesAnyone who can pay
FlexibilitySet resort, set datesMore dates and properties
Best forSqueezing max valueSkipping the sales pitch

One honest wrinkle: some vacpacks also hand you a gift card or resort credit for showing up to the tour. If its a Visa or Mastercard gift card, that's real cash back that widens the gap even more. If its a resort credit, only count it if your actually going to spend it on-site, otherwise its just a number on paper.

Pro Tip: Screenshot the Groupon's total after taxes and resort fees, then compare it to the vacpack's all-in price plus your two hours at the tour. Nine times out of ten the vacpack is cheaper per night, but doing the math yourself keeps either deal from fooling you.

How do you avoid overpaying on either one?

You avoid overpaying by comparing the true all-in total of each deal, not the headline number, becuase both hide costs in different spots. For the Groupon, that means reading the fine print for resort fees and blackout dates before you get excited. For the vacpack, it means confirming the presentation length and the qualifying rules so your not surprised at check-in.

The other trap is booking on emotion. A Groupon countdown timer and a rock-bottom vacpack price both trigger the same grab-it-now reflex, and thats exactly when people skip the math. Me and my wife have a simple habit now: we write down the real total for both, sleep on it one night, and then book. That one night has saved us from more than a few regret purchases.

And if the deal comes with a sweetener, weigh it honestly. A vacpack's Visa gift card is real money that can push it even further ahead of a Groupon, while a resort credit is only worth counting if your going to spend it anyway. Judged that way, the cheaper option is almost always obvious once the drama wears off.

Which should you actually book?

Book the vacpack if you want the lowest possible price and can sit a sales pitch without caving; book the Groupon if a stress-free, no-strings weekend is worth paying extra for. Theres no wrong answer here, it just depends on your tolerance for a pushy hour and a half. I lean vacpack when I want to stretch a small budget and Groupon when I want zero hassle.

If you're leaning vacpack, browse the current lineup on our deals page and compare a few Orlando and Las Vegas options side by side. You can also sort for the cheapest rooms under $100 if you just want the rock-bottom price. Whatever you pick, run the honest math first, then go enjoy the cheap trip you earned.

faqs.answer: On a typical two to four night stay, a vacpack can save $150 to $400 compared to a Groupon getaway, before counting any gift card you receive at the tour.

title: Vacpack vs Paid Travel Club: Which Saves More Money?
metaTitle: Vacpack vs Paid Travel Club Membership | VacationDeals.to
metaDescription: Should you buy a travel club membership or just book vacpacks? Compare the upfront cost, the strings, and which one actually saves you money.
author: The VacationDeals.to Team
bluf: A vacpack costs you $49-$199 and two hours at a presentation, with no long-term commitment. A paid travel club charges hundreds or thousands upfront for ongoing member rates that you have to use alot to break even. For most people who travel a few times a year, stacking cheap vacpacks beats paying a membership fee you might never earn back.
heroImageAlt: A membership card next to a stack of cheap resort booking confirmations
content:
A guy at a home show once tried to sell me a travel club membership for $4,995, and he had a laminated binder and everything. He kept saying I'd save that back in "just a few trips." I did the math on a napkin in the parking lot and realized I'd have to travel like a retired cruise-ship captain to ever come out ahead. Meanwhile I'd booked a $49 vacpack the week before with zero membership card involved.

Bottom Line Up Front: A vacpack costs $49-$199 plus two hours at a presentation, with no long-term commitment. A paid travel club charges hundreds or thousands upfront for ongoing member rates you have to use alot to break even. For most people who travel a few times a year, stacking cheap vacpacks beats a membership fee you might never earn back.

Does a travel club membership actually save money?

A travel club only saves money if you travel often enough to earn back the upfront fee, which is a bigger IF than the salesperson admits. Memberships can cost anywhere from a few hundred dollars to five figures, and the "member rates" have to beat public prices by enough, on enough trips, to cover that sunk cost. If you take two trips a year, the math rarely works.

A vacpack flips the model entirely. Theres no upfront membership, no annual dues, and no pressure to travel constantly just to justify a fee you already paid. You pay $49-$199 per trip, sit one presentation, and walk away owing nothing. The cost is contained to the trip in front of you.

Pay once per trip, or pay to belong forever

What are the strings attached to each?

The string on a vacpack is a single 90-120 minute timeshare presentation per booking, and then your done. The string on a travel club is ongoing: annual dues, booking windows, limited inventory, and the psychological trap of feeling like you have to travel to get your money's worth. One is a short chore, the other is a long-term relationship with your wallet.

Theres also the resale problem. Travel club memberships are notoriously hard to cancel or sell, and alot of people end up stuck paying dues for something they barely use. A vacpack has no resale value because theres nothing to resell, you just used a cheap room and moved on. That's a feature, not a bug.

FactorVacpackPaid Travel Club
Upfront cost$0 membership, $49-$199 per tripHundreds to thousands
Ongoing costNoneOften annual dues
CommitmentOne trip at a timeLong-term, hard to cancel
The catchOne 90-120 min tourBooking limits, dues, breakeven
Best forOccasional travelersVery frequent travelers

To be fair, a heavy traveler who books ten-plus trips a year might squeeze value out of a good club. But that's a narrow slice of people. For everybody else, the membership fee is a bet on future travel you may not actually take, and thats a rough bet to make in a laminated binder under fluorescent lights.

Pro Tip: Before buying any travel club, ask for the exact member rate on a specific date and city, then compare it to a real vacpack for the same trip. If the club can't clearly beat a $49-$199 vacpack after you factor in its fee, walk away and just book the vacpack.

What questions should you ask before buying either?

Before buying a travel club, ask for the exact member price on a real date and city, in writing, so you can compare it to something concrete. Vague promises of up-to-60%-off are meaningless untill you see an actual number next to an actual trip. If the salesperson wont give you a specific quote to take home, thats your answer right there.

For a vacpack, the questions are simpler: how long is the presentation, what are the age and income requirements, and are the dates you want actually available. Theres no membership to scrutinize, just a single trip to confirm. That simplicity is part of why me and my wife keep coming back to vacpacks instead of signing anything long-term.

The deciding question for both is the same: what does this cost me if my travel plans change? A vacpack costs you nothing beyond the one trip. A travel club can keep billing you for years whether you travel or not, and thats the risk that laminated binders never seem to mention.

Which is the smarter money move?

For most travelers, stacking a few vacpacks a year is the smarter move becuase you never pay for access you don't use. You control the cost trip by trip instead of prepaying for savings that only exist if you travel constantly. The travel club only makes sense if you're genuinely on the road a dozen times a year and love the specific inventory.

If you want to test the vacpack path first, look at what's live on our deals page, or start with a low-commitment Branson or Gatlinburg stay to see how the tour-for-a-cheap-room trade feels. You can also filter for deals under $100 to keep your first try nearly risk-free. No card, no dues, no binder.

faqs.answer: They range widely, from a few hundred dollars to well over $10,000 upfront, often plus annual dues. The member rates only save money if you travel enough to cover that cost.

faqs.answer: No. A vacpack is a one-time promotional booking. You pay for the trip, attend one timeshare presentation, and owe nothing afterward.

faqs.answer: Often yes. Many travel clubs are difficult to cancel or resell, which can leave members paying dues for a service they rarely use.

faqs.question: Who benefits most from a travel club?
faqs.answer: Very frequent travelers who take ten or more trips a year and like the club's specific inventory may earn back the fee. Occasional travelers usually do not.

faqs.answer: Yes, and it is a smart test. Book one low-cost vacpack to see how the tour-for-a-cheap-room trade feels before paying any membership fee.

faqs.question: How often would I need to travel to justify a travel club?
faqs.answer: It depends on the fee, but many memberships require several trips a year for many years to break even, which is more than most travelers actually take.

title: Vacpack vs Credit Card Travel Portal: Which Wins?
metaTitle: Vacpack vs Credit Card Travel Portal | VacationDeals.to
metaDescription: Book through your credit card travel portal or grab a vacpack? Compare real prices, points value, and strings to see which one is cheaper.
author: The VacationDeals.to Team
bluf: A credit card travel portal is convenient and lets you burn points, but the cash prices are basically retail. A vacpack is far cheaper in raw dollars if you can sit a presentation. If your points are burning a hole in your pocket the portal is fine, but for pure savings the $49-$199 vacpack usually wins by alot.
heroImageAlt: A credit card next to a laptop showing a hotel booking portal
content:
I have a travel credit card with a fancy portal, and for a while I thought that made me a savvy traveler. Then I priced a three-night Orlando stay in the portal at $612, closed the tab, and booked a $59 Westgate vacpack for basically the same dates. I felt slightly betrayed by my own credit card, which is a wierd emotion to have on a Wednesday.

Bottom Line Up Front: A credit card travel portal is convenient and lets you burn points, but the cash prices are basically retail. A vacpack is far cheaper in raw dollars if you can sit a presentation. If your points are burning a hole in your pocket, the portal is fine, but for pure savings the $49-$199 vacpack usually wins by alot.

Is a credit card travel portal cheaper than a vacpack?

No, a credit card travel portal is almost never cheaper than a vacpack when you compare cash prices. Portals sell rooms at close to public retail rates, so a resort stay might run $400-$700 for a few nights, while a vacpack lands the same kind of trip at $49-$199. The portal's real perk is convenience and the ability to spend points, not a lower sticker price.

Where the portal shines is flexibility and simplicity. You book in two minutes, theres no tour, and you can use it anywhere. A vacpack asks more of you up front, a presentation and some qualifying requirements, but it pays you back with a much lower price. Its a classic effort-versus-cost trade.

Points feel free until you price the room

Do points make the portal a better deal?

Points only make the portal a better deal if you already have them and value them at a decent redemption rate, otherwise your just paying retail with extra steps. Card portals often value points at around one cent each, which is fine but not amazing, and the underlying room price is still high. If you're paying cash out of pocket either way, the vacpack is the cheaper cash trip almost every time.

Theres also the honesty issue with "free" points. Points arent free, you earned them through spending, so burning them on an overpriced portal room isnt a win, its just spending a different currency. Me and my wife try to save points for flights, where they stretch further, and use vacpacks for the cheap resort nights.

FactorVacpackCard Travel Portal
Typical cash price$49-$199 for 2-5 nights$400-$700 for a similar stay
PointsNot applicableCan redeem, often ~1 cent each
The catch90-120 min timeshare tourRetail-level cash pricing
ConvenienceSome requirements to qualifyBook in a couple minutes
Best forLowest cash costBurning points, zero hassle

One more thing worth saying plainly: some vacpacks throw in a gift card or resort credit at the tour. A Visa gift card is real money that effectively lowers your trip cost even further, while a resort credit only counts if you'd spend it there anyway. Portals dont hand you cash back like that, they just give you a room.

Pro Tip: Price your exact trip in your card portal, then check the same city and dates as a vacpack. If the portal costs more in cash even after your point discount, the vacpack is the better deal, and you can save those points for a flight where they stretch further.

How do you get the most from each option?

You get the most from a card portal by saving your points for redemptions where they punch above one cent each, which usually means flights, not overpriced portal rooms. Burning points on a retail-priced resort night is the weakest way to use them. Treat the portal as a convenience tool, not a savings engine, and it earns its place.

You get the most from a vacpack by going in prepared to say no and by picking a destination you'd genuinely visit anyway. The cheap room is only a deal if you actually want the trip, otherwise your just buying a bargain you didnt need. Me and my wife only book vacpacks for places already on our list, which keeps the savings real.

Stacked together, the two are stronger than either alone. Points cover the flight, the vacpack covers the room, and any Visa gift card from the tour covers a dinner or two. Thats a genuinely cheap trip, and it uses each tool for what its actually good at instead of forcing one to do everything.

Which should you use for your next trip?

Use a vacpack when you want the cheapest possible cash trip and can handle a presentation; use the portal when you have points to burn or you value pure convenience over price. They actually pair well, points for the flight, vacpack for the room. Theres no need to treat it as either-or on every single trip.

If the cash savings are what you're after, scan our deals page and compare a few Las Vegas or Orlando vacpacks against whatever your portal quotes. Even a quick look at deals under $100 will show you how big the cash gap can get. Then decide where your points do the most good.

faqs.answer: Usually yes, in cash terms. Portals sell rooms near retail, often $400-$700 for a few nights, while a vacpack costs $49-$199 for a similar stay in exchange for attending a presentation.

faqs.answer: Many card portals value points at roughly one cent each. That is decent but does not lower the underlying room price, which is typically close to retail.

faqs.question: Should I use points for a resort room or a flight?
faqs.answer: Points often stretch further on flights than on portal hotel rooms. Many travelers save points for airfare and use vacpacks for the cheap resort nights.

faqs.answer: No. A vacpack is a cash promotional booking and does not accept points. Its savings come from the low price plus any gift card at the tour.

faqs.question: What is the trade-off with a vacpack?
faqs.answer: You must attend a 90 to 120 minute timeshare presentation and meet age and income requirements. In return you get a room far below retail price.

faqs.question: Is a credit card travel portal ever the better choice?
faqs.answer: Yes, when you have points to burn or you value fast, no-strings booking. For pure cash savings, though, the vacpack usually wins.

faqs.question: Can a vacpack include cash back?
faqs.answer: Some do, in the form of a Visa or Mastercard gift card for completing the tour. That is real money that lowers your trip cost further, unlike a portal booking.

faqs.answer: Yes. A common strategy is using points for the flight through your card portal and a vacpack for the discounted resort room.

faqs.question: Are card portal prices negotiable?
faqs.answer: No, portal prices are fixed at what the card issuer displays. To pay less in cash, compare the same trip as a vacpack.

title: Florida vs Mexico Vacpack: Which Is the Better Deal?
metaTitle: Florida vs Mexico Vacpack: Better Deal | VacationDeals.to
metaDescription: Florida or Mexico for your vacpack? Compare prices, all-inclusive value, travel costs, and which one gives you more vacation per dollar.
author: The VacationDeals.to Team
bluf: A Florida vacpack is cheaper up front, often $49-$199, and easy to reach if you can drive. A Mexico vacpack costs more, roughly $149-$999, but it's usually all-inclusive, so food and drinks are baked in. If you can drive to Florida it's the budget king, but for an all-in beach blowout Mexico can be the better total value.
heroImageAlt: Split view of an Orlando resort pool and a Cancun beach with turquoise water
content:
Last year I couldnt decide between a $59 Orlando vacpack and a $299 all-inclusive in Cancun, so I made a spreadsheet, which is exactly the kind of person I've become. The Orlando number was tiny and the Cancun number scared me, until I remembered Cancun included every meal and margarita. Suddenly the scary number got alot more reasonable.

Bottom Line Up Front: A Florida vacpack is cheaper up front, often $49-$199, and easy to reach if you can drive. A Mexico vacpack costs more, roughly $149-$999, but it's usually all-inclusive, so food and drinks are baked in. If you can drive to Florida its the budget king, but for an all-in beach blowout Mexico can be the better total value.

Is a Florida or Mexico vacpack cheaper?

A Florida vacpack is cheaper on the sticker, typically $49-$199, while a Mexico vacpack runs roughly $149-$999. But the sticker doesnt tell the whole story, becuase Mexico deals are usually all-inclusive and Florida deals are room-only. Once you add up food, drinks, and a flight, the gap narrows and sometimes flips depending on how you travel.

The other big variable is how you get there. A ton of people can drive to Florida, which keeps the trip genuinely cheap. Mexico almost always means flying, plus passports and airport transfers, so the total cost climbs even when the room itself is a good price. Distance is the quiet tiebreaker here.

Cheap and drivable, or all-inclusive and far

Does Mexico's all-inclusive change the math?

Yes, an all-inclusive Mexico vacpack changes the math a lot because it folds your food and drinks into one price. In Florida you're paying for the room only, so three days of meals, snacks, and drinks can quietly add $150-$300 to the trip. In Cancun that spend is already inside the $149-$999 you paid, which makes a scarier sticker feel a lot more honest by the end.

That said, all-inclusive value only counts if you actually eat and drink at the resort. If your the type who wants to explore local taco stands and skip resort buffets, you're paying for meals you wont use. Me and my wife lean all-inclusive because we genuinely park at the pool bar, but thats a personal thing, not a universal win.

FactorFlorida VacpackMexico Vacpack
Typical price$49-$199 (room only)$149-$999 (often all-inclusive)
Food and drinksPaid separatelyUsually included
Getting thereDrivable for manyFlight, passport, transfers
Best vibeTheme parks, easy budgetBeach, all-in relaxation
The catch90-120 min tour, room only90-120 min tour, farther travel

Both come with the same core string: a 90-120 minute timeshare presentation. And both sometimes toss in a gift card or resort credit for showing up. As always, a Visa gift card is real cash and a resort credit only counts if you spend it there, so dont let a credit trick you into thinking a pricier deal is cheaper than it is.

Pro Tip: If you can drive to Florida, price it room-only and add your real food budget. Then price the Mexico all-inclusive with the flight. Compare the two totals, not the two stickers, becuase the all-inclusive often closes a gap that looked huge at first glance.

What hidden costs should you plan for?

The hidden costs are different on each side, so plan for the right ones. In Florida, budget for meals, parking, and theme-park tickets, becuase the cheap room doesnt cover any of that. Those add-ons can quietly turn a $59 room into a much bigger week if your not tracking them from the start.

In Mexico, the room may be all-inclusive, but the trip still isnt. Flights, passport fees, airport transfers, and tips add up, and some resorts push paid upgrade experiences once your on-site. The all-inclusive price is honest about food and drinks, but it wont cover the plane ticket or the excursion you'll inevitably want to book.

The fix for both is the same boring, effective habit: list every real cost before you book, not after. Me and my wife tally travel, food, and extras for each option on one screen, then compare the two grand totals. Its unglamorous, but it keeps a scary sticker or a tiny one from making the decision for us.

Which one should you book?

Book Florida if you want the lowest total cost and can drive; book Mexico if you want a hands-off, all-inclusive beach trip and dont mind flying. For a family doing theme parks on a tight budget, Florida is tough to beat. For a couples getaway where you just want everything handled, Mexico's all-inclusive earns its higher price.

Compare live options on our deals page, peek at Orlando for the budget route, and check Cancun if the all-inclusive life is calling. You can also filter deals under $100 if raw price is your only metric. Either way, compare totals, then go get some sun.

faqs.question: Is a Florida vacpack cheaper than a Mexico vacpack?
faqs.answer: On the sticker, yes. Florida vacpacks run $49-$199 room-only, while Mexico vacpacks run about $149-$999 but are usually all-inclusive, which narrows the real gap.

faqs.question: Are Mexico vacpacks all-inclusive?
faqs.answer: Most are. A Mexico vacpack typically includes food and drinks in the price, while a Florida vacpack is usually room-only with meals paid separately.

faqs.answer: Yes. Traveling to Mexico requires a valid passport, and you should also budget for flights and airport transfers, which add to the total trip cost.

faqs.question: Which is better for a family trip?
faqs.answer: Florida is often better for families on a budget, especially for theme parks, because it is drivable for many and has low room-only prices. Mexico suits couples wanting an all-inclusive beach trip.

faqs.question: Does the all-inclusive really save money?
faqs.answer: It can, if you eat and drink at the resort. An all-inclusive folds meals and drinks into one price, which can save $150-$300 versus paying separately in Florida.

faqs.answer: Yes. Both Florida and Mexico vacpacks require a 90 to 120 minute timeshare presentation to unlock the discounted price.

faqs.answer: Because Florida vacpacks are room-only, three or four days of meals, snacks, and drinks can add roughly $150-$300 to the total trip cost.

faqs.question: Can I get a gift card with either one?
faqs.answer: Sometimes. Both may include a gift card or resort credit for completing the tour. A Visa gift card is real cash, while a resort credit only helps if you spend it on-site.

faqs.question: Which has lower travel costs?
faqs.answer: Florida usually does, because many travelers can drive there. Mexico almost always requires flights, a passport, and transfers, which raise the total cost.

title: All-Inclusive vs Room-Only Vacpack: Which Is Worth It?
metaDescription: All-inclusive or room-only vacpack? See the real per-day math on food and drinks and learn which one is actually the better value for your trip.
author: The VacationDeals.to Team
bluf: A room-only vacpack is dirt cheap up front, often $49-$199, but you pay for every meal and drink on top. An all-inclusive vacpack costs more, around $149-$999, with food and drinks baked in. If you'll eat and drink at the resort, all-inclusive usually wins; if you plan to explore and eat out, room-only keeps your total lower.
heroImageAlt: A resort buffet spread next to a simple hotel room key card
content:
The first time I booked a room-only vacpack, I felt so smart about the $49 price that I completely forgot humans need to eat. Three days later I'd spent $214 on food, including one truly regrettable $19 poolside nacho situation. That trip taught me that "room only" is a price tag with a hungry asterisk attached.

Bottom Line Up Front: A room-only vacpack is dirt cheap up front, often $49-$199, but you pay for every meal and drink on top. An all-inclusive vacpack costs more, around $149-$999, with food and drinks baked in. If you'll eat and drink at the resort, all-inclusive usually wins; if you plan to explore and eat out, room-only keeps your total lower.

Is an all-inclusive vacpack worth the higher price?

An all-inclusive vacpack is worth it when your meals and drinks at the resort would cost more than the price difference, which happens faster than most people expect. A couple can easily spend $80-$150 a day on food and drinks, so on a three-night trip that's $240-$450 you're not tracking. If the all-inclusive upgrade costs less than that, it's genuinely the better value.

Room-only wins in the opposite case: short stays, light eaters, or trips where you plan to be out exploring anyway. If your going to spend the days at theme parks or wandering a town, you wont use a resort meal plan enough to justify it. The right answer really does depend on how you actually vacation.

The room is cheap, the nachos are not

How do I figure out which one saves me money?

Estimate your honest daily food and drink spend, multiply by nights, and compare that to the price gap between the two vacpacks. If room-only is $59 and all-inclusive is $299 for three nights, the gap is $240, or $80 a day. If you'd spend more than $80 a day eating and drinking anyway, the all-inclusive is cheaper in disguise. If you'd spend less, room-only wins.

The mistake people make is comparing the two stickers instead of the two totals. A $49 room looks unbeatable untill you add four days of meals to it. Me and my wife now run this little calculation every time, becuase the cheap sticker fooled us more than once before we wised up.

FactorRoom-Only VacpackAll-Inclusive Vacpack
Sticker price$49-$199$149-$999
Food and drinksPaid separately, $80-$150/dayIncluded in the price
Best forExplorers, light eaters, short staysPoolside relaxers, families, longer stays
RiskFood costs balloon the totalPaying for meals you skip
The catch90-120 min tour90-120 min tour

Both types share the same trade: a 90-120 minute timeshare presentation to unlock the price. And both may include a gift card or resort credit at the tour. Keep the cash-versus-credit rule in mind, a Visa gift card lowers your real cost while a resort credit only counts if you'd have spent it there, otherwise its just a marketing number.

Pro Tip: Add one honest line to your budget before booking: your realistic daily food and drink spend times the number of nights. If that number beats the all-inclusive upgrade cost, book all-inclusive. If it doesnt, book room-only and eat out. Its a two-minute calculation that routinely saves real money.

Does trip style matter more than price?

Yes, your trip style often matters more than the sticker price, becuase the wrong fit wastes money no matter how cheap the deal looked. A poolside relaxer who books room-only ends up nickel-and-dimed on food, while an explorer who books all-inclusive pays for buffets they skip to go eat tacos in town. The best value is the one that matches how you actually spend your days.

So before you compare numbers, be honest about the trip. Are you the type to camp at the swim-up bar, or the type who's out from breakfast to dinner? Theres no wrong answer, but pretending you'll behave differently on vacation than you always do is how people overpay. My wife and I know we're pool people, so all-inclusive usually wins for us.

Once you've named your style, the money math gets easy. Match the format to your habits first, then run the food-cost comparison to confirm it. That order, style then price, keeps you from booking a deal that looks great on paper but fights how you like to travel.

So which should you pick?

Pick all-inclusive if you'll relax at the resort and eat there, and pick room-only if you're an explorer, a light eater, or on a very short trip. Neither is universally better, it comes down to your eating style and how much time you'll actually spend on-property. Be honest with yourself, becuase the wrong pick quietly costs money either way.

See both styles live on our deals page, compare an all-inclusive Cancun stay against a room-only Orlando one, and use the under $100 filter if you want to start room-only. Run your food math first, then book the one that fits how you really travel.

title: Resort Preview Deal vs No-Strings Hotel Sale: Which to Book?
metaTitle: Resort Preview Deal vs No-Strings Hotel Sale | VacationDeals.to
metaDescription: A resort preview vacpack has a tour; a no-strings hotel sale does not. Compare the price, the catch, and which one is truly worth it for you.
author: The VacationDeals.to Team
bluf: A resort preview deal gives you a much cheaper room, $49-$199, in exchange for a 90-120 minute presentation. A no-strings hotel sale skips the tour but the discount is smaller, so you pay more per night. If you value your time over money, take the hotel sale; if you value money over a morning, the preview deal wins.
heroImageAlt: A resort tour sign next to a hotel sale banner
content:
My neighbor swears he'd never sit a timeshare tour, so he booked a "no-strings" hotel sale for his anniversary and paid $340 for two nights. I booked a resort preview deal at a nicer property for $59, sat a tour, said no six times, and had money left for a fancy dinner. He still says he got the better deal. He did not get the better deal.

Bottom Line Up Front: A resort preview deal gives you a much cheaper room, $49-$199, in exchange for a 90-120 minute presentation. A no-strings hotel sale skips the tour but the discount is smaller, so you pay more per night. If you value your time over money take the hotel sale, and if you value money over a morning the preview deal wins.

What is the difference between a resort preview deal and a hotel sale?

The core difference is the tour: a resort preview deal requires a 90-120 minute timeshare presentation, while a no-strings hotel sale requires nothing but your payment. That single trade is why the preview deal can charge $49-$199 for a stay that a hotel sale would price at $200-$500. One sells you a room and hopes to sell you more, the other just sells you a room.

Neither is dishonest, they just make money differently. The hotel sale earns its margin on the room. The preview deal loses money on the room on purpose, betting a slice of guests will buy a timeshare after seeing the property. You're not doing anything shady by saying no, thats a completely normal outcome they've already priced in.

Two hours of your time, or two hundred dollars

Is skipping the tour worth paying more?

Skipping the tour is worth it only if your time is genuinely worth more than the money you'd save, which for most casual travelers it isnt. The preview deal typically saves $150-$400 versus a comparable no-strings sale, in exchange for about two hours. That's a high hourly rate for sitting in a chair and repeating "no thank you," so the math usually favors the tour.

The real reason people pay more to skip it is discomfort, not economics. A sales pitch is definately annoying, and some folks cave under pressure. If you know you'll say yes to something you dont want, then yeah, paying to avoid the room is rational, and thats a seperate calculation entirely. But if you can hold a polite no, your basically getting paid a couple hundred bucks for a boring morning.

FactorResort Preview DealNo-Strings Hotel Sale
Typical price$49-$199$200-$500 for a similar stay
The catch90-120 min timeshare tourNone, just pay
RequirementsUsually 25+, ~$50K income, couplesAnyone who can pay
Time costAbout two hours on-siteZero
Best forSaving real moneyProtecting your time and calm

Preview deals also sometimes sweeten the pot with a gift card or resort credit for attending. Thats extra value on top of the already-lower room, but only count a resort credit if you'd spend it there anyway. A Visa gift card, on the other hand, is straight cash back that a no-strings hotel sale simply doesnt offer.

Pro Tip: Before assuming you'd cave at a presentation, remember the golden rule: you can say no as many times as it takes, and you still keep the deal. Go in with a firm, friendly "we're just here for the getaway" and treat the two hours as a paid errand, becuase thats exactly what it is.

How do you survive the presentation without caving?

You survive the presentation by deciding your answer before you walk in and treating the whole thing as a paid errand. Go in knowing you're there for the getaway, not to buy, and repeat a calm, friendly no-thank-you as many times as it takes. The deal is yours as long as you attend, not as long as you say yes.

It helps to remember the salesperson isnt your enemy, they're just doing a job with a script. You dont owe them a purchase, an excuse, or even a long explanation. Me and my wife bring water, treat it like a slightly boring meeting, and remind each other beforehand that the low price is already earned the moment we sit down.

If you genuinely worry you'll crack under pressure, thats useful self-knowledge, and it might mean the no-strings hotel sale is worth the premium for you. But for most people, two hours of polite declining is a very well-paid way to spend a morning. Know yourself, then pick the option that fits how you handle a pitch.

Which one should you choose?

Choose the resort preview deal if you want to save real money and can sit a pitch without buying; choose the no-strings hotel sale if a calm, tour-free trip is worth the premium to you. Be honest about which kind of person you are under sales pressure. The preview deal is the better value for anyone who can hold a polite no.

If the savings sound good, browse current preview deals on our deals page, or look at a specific spot like Gatlinburg or Branson to see how low the price really goes. The under $100 filter shows the boldest examples. Weigh your time against the dollars, then book the one that fits your temperament.

title: East Coast vs West Coast Vacpack: Where's the Better Deal?
metaTitle: East Coast vs West Coast Vacpack | VacationDeals.to
metaDescription: East coast or west coast vacpack? Compare prices, destinations, travel costs, and which coast gives you more vacation for $49-$199.
author: The VacationDeals.to Team
bluf: East coast vacpacks lean toward Orlando, Branson, Gatlinburg, and Williamsburg, usually $49-$199 and easy to drive to for a lot of the country. West coast options center on Las Vegas at similar low prices. The cheaper coast is really whichever one you can reach without an expensive flight, so let your home base decide.
heroImageAlt: Map showing east coast resort towns and west coast Las Vegas strip
content:
I grew up on the east coast and assumed all the good vacpacks were near me, which is a very east-coast thing to assume. Then a buddy in Arizona booked a $49 Vegas vacpack, drove four hours, and had a better time than my last three trips combined. Turns out the best coast for a vacpack is mostly just the one you dont have to fly across the country to reach.

Bottom Line Up Front: East coast vacpacks lean toward Orlando, Branson, Gatlinburg, and Williamsburg, usually $49-$199 and drivable for a lot of the country. West coast options center on Las Vegas at similar low prices. The cheaper coast is really whichever one you can reach without an expensive flight, so let your home base decide.

Which coast has cheaper vacpacks?

Neither coast is reliably cheaper on the room itself, becuase both offer vacpacks in the $49-$199 range; the real cost difference is how far you have to travel. The east coast has more vacpack destinations spread out, Orlando, Gatlinburg, Branson, Williamsburg, Myrtle Beach, while the west coast concentrates hard around Las Vegas. So the winner depends on which cluster sits closer to you.

Because room prices are similar, travel cost becomes the tiebreaker. A $49 room that needs a $350 cross-country flight isnt a $49 trip anymore, its a $399 trip. Whoever can drive to their coast's deals wins, and thats usually the coast they already live near. Geography does most of the deciding here.

Same cheap room, very different plane ticket

What destinations does each coast offer?

The east coast offers the widest spread of vacpack towns, while the west coast is dominated by Las Vegas. On the east side you can pick theme-park Orlando, mountain Gatlinburg, showtime Branson, historic Williamsburg, or beachy Myrtle Beach. Out west, Vegas is the powerhouse, with its cheap $49 vacpacks and nonstop entertainment doing most of the heavy lifting.

That difference in variety matters depending on your vibe. If you want options and might drive between a couple of spots, the east coast gives you more to work with. If you just want one big, all-in-one destination where theres always something happening, Vegas is honestly hard to beat. There both strong, they just serve different moods.

FactorEast Coast VacpackWest Coast Vacpack
Typical price$49-$199$49-$199
Top destinationsOrlando, Gatlinburg, Branson, WilliamsburgLas Vegas
VarietyMany towns and vibesOne big powerhouse city
Best forDrivers in the East/MidwestDrivers in the West/Southwest
The catch90-120 min tour90-120 min tour

The presentation requirement is identical on both coasts, a 90-120 minute tour, and both regions sometimes include a gift card or resort credit for attending. Same honesty rule everywhere: a Visa gift card is real cash you can put toward gas or a flight, while a resort credit only counts if your going to spend it on-site anyway.

Pro Tip: Dont anchor on the coast you grew up near. Price a vacpack on both coasts with your real travel cost added, becuase a drivable $49 Vegas trip can beat a $49 Orlando trip that needs a plane ticket, and vice versa. Let the total, not the postcard, pick your coast.

How does your home base change the answer?

Your home base changes the answer more than almost anything, becuase it decides whether a deal is a short drive or a pricey flight. Someone in Atlanta can turn a $49 Orlando or Gatlinburg vacpack into a genuinely cheap weekend, while someone in Denver gets that same value from a drivable Vegas run. The room price barely moves; your zip code does the real work.

That's why copying a friend's best-deal rarely works. The trip that was a bargain for them might be a flight-and-rental-car ordeal for you. My cousin raves about east-coast vacpacks, but from where he lives they're all a tank of gas away, so of course they feel cheap to him.

The move is to run the numbers from your own driveway, every time. Add your real travel cost to each coast's room price and compare the totals, not the stickers. Do that and the right coast usually picks itself, and it wont always be the one you assumed growing up.

So which coast should you book?

Book the coast you can drive to, because with room prices this similar, the flight is what decides the real cost. East-coasters and Midwesterners usually win with Orlando, Gatlinburg, or Branson, while folks out west get more value from Las Vegas. If you can drive to either, pick the destination that matches your mood.

Compare both on our deals page, then dig into Las Vegas for the west or Orlando and Branson for the east. The under $100 filter shows how low each coast can go. Add your travel cost, compare totals, and let your driveway pick the winner.

title: Chain-Hotel Vacpack vs Independent Resort: Which Is Better?
metaTitle: Chain-Hotel vs Independent Resort Vacpack | VacationDeals.to
metaDescription: Chain-hotel vacpack or independent resort? Compare consistency, amenities, price, and which one gives you a better cheap stay in 2026.
author: The VacationDeals.to Team
bluf: A chain-hotel vacpack gives you predictable rooms, known amenities, and a familiar brand, usually $49-$249. An independent resort can offer more character and sometimes bigger units at a similar price, but quality varies more. If you want a safe, known experience go chain; if you want personality and can handle some variance, go independent.
heroImageAlt: A branded chain resort tower next to a boutique independent resort
content:
I once booked an independent resort vacpack purely because the photos had a tiki bar, and I am powerless against a tiki bar. It turned out great, but my sister booked a different independent spot the same month and got a room that smelled faintly of boat. That's the independent gamble in a nutshell: sometimes tiki paradise, sometimes mystery boat smell.

Bottom Line Up Front: A chain-hotel vacpack gives you predictable rooms, known amenities, and a familiar brand, usually $49-$249. An independent resort can offer more character and sometimes bigger units at a similar price, but quality varies more. If you want a safe known experience go chain, and if you want personality and can handle some variance go independent.

Is a chain-hotel vacpack more reliable than an independent resort?

Yes, a chain-hotel vacpack is generally more reliable becuase big brands enforce consistent standards across properties. When you book a known chain, you have a decent idea of the room size, the cleanliness bar, and the amenities before you arrive. An independent resort has no such guarantee, so the experience swings more from great to disappointing depending on the specific property.

That reliability is the whole appeal of a chain. Westgate, HGV, and similar brands run vacpacks in the $49-$249 range, and part of what your paying for is knowing roughly what you'll get. For a lot of travelers, especially first-timers, that predictability is worth more than a shot at something with more personality.

Predictable comfort, or a room with a personality

Do independent resorts offer better value?

Independent resorts can offer better value when they throw in bigger units, unique settings, or extras a chain wouldnt, but the value is less predictable. Some independents give you a huge condo-style unit or a killer location for the same $49-$199 a chain charges for a standard room. Others cut corners you wont see untill check-in, which is the risk you accept for the upside.

The smart move with an independent is homework. Read recent guest photos and reviews, not just the glossy listing shots, becuase the listing is trying to sell you a tiki bar. Me and my wife have scored amazing independent stays this way, and dodged a few boat-smell situations too. The value is real, it just takes more digging to find safely.

FactorChain-Hotel VacpackIndependent Resort
Typical price$49-$249$49-$199
ConsistencyHigh, brand standardsVaries by property
Room sizeUsually standardSometimes larger condo-style
CharacterFamiliar and predictableMore unique, hit or miss
The catch90-120 min tour90-120 min tour, do your homework

Both chain and independent vacpacks run the same 90-120 minute presentation, and both can include a gift card or resort credit for attending. As always, judge the sweetener honestly: a Visa gift card is real cash back, while a resort credit is only worth counting if you'll actually spend it on-site during your stay.

Pro Tip: For an independent resort, ignore the professional listing photos and hunt down recent guest photos and reviews instead. Five minutes of real-guest snooping is the difference between a big condo with a tiki bar and a standard room that smells like a marina.

How do you research an independent resort safely?

You research an independent resort safely by trusting recent guest evidence over the property's own marketing. Sort reviews by newest, scan for repeated complaints about cleanliness or surprise fees, and hunt down guest-uploaded photos that show what the rooms really look like. The glossy listing shots are selling you a fantasy; the phone snaps in the reviews are telling you the truth.

Pay special attention to how a resort responds to bad reviews, becuase that tells you how they'll treat you if something goes wrong. A place that answers complaints politely and fixes problems is a safer bet than one that argues with every unhappy guest. Me and my wife have talked ourselves out of a few great-deals purely from reading the owner's defensive replies.

With a chain, you can skip most of this becuase the brand standard does the vetting for you. Thats the quiet luxury of booking a known name: less homework, fewer surprises. The independent can absolutely win on value, but only if your willing to put in the ten minutes of digging that keeps the gamble smart.

Which type should you book?

Book a chain-hotel vacpack if you want a safe, predictable stay with no surprises, and book an independent resort if you want more character and are willing to research to avoid a dud. First-timers usually do best starting with a known chain. Once your comfortable with how vacpacks work, branching out to a well-reviewed independent can pay off nicely.

Compare both on our deals page, check a big-brand option like Westgate, and browse destinations like Orlando where both chains and independents compete. The under $100 filter works for either type. Do a little homework, then book the stay that matches how much surprise you can handle.

title: Booking a Vacpack vs Waiting for a Flash Sale: Which Wins?
metaTitle: Book a Vacpack Now vs Wait for a Flash Sale | VacationDeals.to
metaDescription: Should you book a vacpack now or hold out for a flash sale? See how the prices really compare and which strategy saves more in 2026.
author: The VacationDeals.to Team
bluf: Vacpacks are already priced like a permanent flash sale, $49-$199, so waiting for a bigger hotel flash sale usually means chasing a discount that lands above what a vacpack already charges. If you have flexible dates and love a gamble, watch flash sales, but for guaranteed low pricing right now, booking the vacpack is the safer win.
heroImageAlt: A calendar with a booking date circled next to a flash sale countdown timer
content:
I once waited three weeks for a flash sale on a beach resort, refreshing the site like a raccoon guarding a trash can, convinced I'd score something legendary. The sale finally hit, the room dropped to $289, and I just sat there, becuase I already had a $59 vacpack booked for the same week. The flash sale I'd been stalking was more expensive than the deal I already had.

Bottom Line Up Front: Vacpacks are already priced like a permanent flash sale, $49-$199, so waiting for a bigger hotel flash sale usually means chasing a discount that lands above what a vacpack already charges. If you have flexible dates and love a gamble watch the flash sales, but for guaranteed low pricing right now, booking the vacpack is the safer win.

Is it better to book a vacpack now or wait for a flash sale?

For most travelers its better to book the vacpack now, becuase vacpacks are already discounted far below the prices most flash sales ever reach. A hotel flash sale might knock a room down to $250-$400, which feels exciting untill you realize a vacpack was $49-$199 the whole time. Waiting mostly risks losing the low price you could lock in today.

Flash sales create urgency on purpose, which makes a so-so discount feel like a jackpot. But urgency isnt savings. The vacpack skips the countdown-timer theater and just gives you a low price, in exchange for a presentation. If you compare the actual numbers instead of the drama, the vacpack usually already won.

The best flash sale is the one already on the table

When does waiting for a flash sale actually pay off?

Waiting for a flash sale pays off mainly when you want a no-tour stay, have totally flexible dates, and are willing to miss out if the sale never comes. Flash sales can occasionally beat normal hotel rates for a specific weekend, and they dont require sitting a presentation. If avoiding the tour matters more to you than rock-bottom pricing, patience can be worth it.

The catch is that flash sales are unpredictable, and while your waiting, prices and availability move. Me and my wife have watched a "sale" arrive for dates we couldnt use, which is the whole trap. A vacpack is a bird in the hand; a flash sale is a bird thats emailing you a countdown timer and might not show up at all.

FactorBook a Vacpack NowWait for a Flash Sale
Typical price$49-$199, available now$250-$400 when a sale hits
CertaintyLocked in todayMight never come for your dates
The catch90-120 min timeshare tourNo tour, but higher price
Date flexibilityBook set dates nowMust stay flexible and wait
Best forGuaranteed low priceNo-tour stays, patient gamblers

Vacpacks also sometimes include a gift card or resort credit at the tour, which flash sales dont offer at all. Keep the usual rule in mind: a Visa gift card is real cash that lowers your true cost, while a resort credit only counts if your going to spend it on the property during your trip.

Pro Tip: If you're tempted to wait for a flash sale, set a price target first, like "I'll wait only if I think it'll beat $150." Since vacpacks routinely sit at $49-$199, that target is hard for a flash sale to hit, which usually settles the debate in the vacpack's favor.

What does waiting really cost you?

Waiting really costs you certainty, and sometimes the trip itself, becuase prices and availability dont sit still while you refresh a sale page. The dates you wanted can sell out, the resort you liked can fill up, and the flash sale you were promised can arrive for a random weekend you cant use. All that risk buys you a discount thats usually still higher than a vacpack.

Theres also a hidden emotional cost to the waiting game: it turns a fun trip into a chore of tab-refreshing and second-guessing. I've spent evenings stalking a sale that never beat the vacpack I could've booked in two minutes. Thats time and mental energy I'll never get back, all for a worse price.

None of this means flash sales are useless, they just work best for flexible travelers who dont mind missing out. If a locked-in low price matters to you at all, the vacpack removes the entire gamble. You know the cost, you know the dates, and you can stop refreshing and start packing.

Which strategy should you use?

Use the book-now vacpack strategy if you want a guaranteed low price and can sit a presentation; wait for a flash sale only if a tour-free stay and flexible dates matter more than saving the most money. For pure savings and certainty, booking the vacpack today beats gambling on a sale that may land higher, later, or never.

title: $99 Vacpack vs Cashing In Hotel Points: Which Is Smarter?
metaTitle: $99 Vacpack vs Cashing In Hotel Points | VacationDeals.to
metaDescription: Spend $99 on a vacpack or burn your hotel points? Compare the real value per point and which move gives you a cheaper resort stay.
author: The VacationDeals.to Team
bluf: A $99 vacpack keeps your hard-earned points in the bank and costs less than one night's worth of most point redemptions. Cashing in hotel points feels free but often burns 15,000-30,000 points per night for value you could've bought for $99. Unless your points are about to expire, the vacpack is usually the smarter move and saves your points for pricier trips.
heroImageAlt: A ninety-nine dollar deal tag next to a phone showing a hotel points balance
content:
I had 60,000 hotel points sitting in an account and treated them like Monopoly money, ready to blow them on a beach weekend. Right before I hit redeem, I noticed a $99 vacpack for basically the same trip. I did some quick math and realized burning those points would've been like paying $600 for something I could get for $99. I closed the app and felt weirdly protective of my little point stash.

Bottom Line Up Front: A $99 vacpack keeps your hard-earned points in the bank and costs less than one night's worth of most point redemptions. Cashing in hotel points feels free but often burns 15,000-30,000 points per night for value you could've bought for $99. Unless your points are about to expire, the vacpack is usually the smarter move and saves your points for pricier trips.

Is a $99 vacpack cheaper than using hotel points?

In real terms, yes, a $99 vacpack is usually cheaper than burning points on the same kind of stay. A resort night booked with points often costs 15,000-30,000 points, and at a typical value of around one cent per point, thats $150-$300 of value gone for one night. A $99 vacpack gets you multiple nights for less than that, without touching your balance.

The reason this feels backwards is that points seem free. There not free, you earned them through spending, so using them still has a real cost, its just hidden. When you compare the dollar value of the points you'd burn against a $99 vacpack, the vacpack almost always comes out ahead per night.

Ninety-nine dollars now, or points you cant get back

When does cashing in hotel points make sense?

Cashing in points makes sense when they're about to expire, when you want a stay with zero tour, or when the redemption value is unusually high. Points that expire unused are worth exactly zero, so burning them on any decent trip beats losing them. And some premium redemptions genuinely stretch points past two cents each, which can beat a vacpack for that specific booking.

Theres also the tour factor. A $99 vacpack requires a 90-120 minute presentation, and points redemptions dont. If you flat-out wont sit a pitch, points buy you a tour-free stay, and that convenience has real value. Me and my wife save points for exactly these moments, expiring balances or trips where we want zero hassle.

Factor$99 VacpackCashing In Hotel Points
Cash cost$99 for the stay$0 cash, but points spent
Point costNoneOften 15,000-30,000 per night
Hidden value burnedNone~$150-$300 per night at 1 cent/point
The catch90-120 min timeshare tourNo tour, but points gone
Best forSaving points, lowest real costExpiring points, tour-free stays

And dont forget vacpacks sometimes hand you a gift card or resort credit at the tour, which makes that $99 stretch even further. Points redemptions give you a room and nothing else. Same honesty rule as always: a Visa gift card is real cash back, while a resort credit only counts if your actually going to spend it during the trip.

Pro Tip: Do the point math before you redeem: multiply the points a stay costs by one cent to see its rough dollar value. If a night costs 25,000 points, thats about $250 of value for one night, and a $99 vacpack blows that away. Save the points for a flight or a pricey trip where they stretch further.

How do you value points before you spend them?

You value points before spending by turning them into a rough dollar figure, so a free night stops feeling free and starts feeling like the real cost it is. Multiply the points a stay requires by about one cent, and suddenly a 25,000-point night reads as roughly $250. Held up against a $99 vacpack, most cheap-room redemptions look like a bad trade instantly.

This little habit reframes every redemption decision. Instead of asking do-I-have-enough-points, you start asking whether this is the best $250 of value you can get from them. For a cheap resort weekend, the answer is almost always no, becuase a vacpack does it for less cash than the points are worth.

Save the points for where they genuinely shine: expensive flights, peak-season stays, or premium redemptions that stretch past two cents each. My wife and I treat our balance like an emergency fund for pricey trips, not spare change for rooms we could buy for $99. Value them first, and you'll spend them alot more wisely.

Which move should you make?

Make the $99 vacpack move when you want the lowest real cost and your points arent expiring; cash in points when they're about to vanish, when you refuse to sit a tour, or when a redemption is unusually valuable. For everyday cheap resort trips, the vacpack wins and quietly protects your point balance for bigger, better uses later.

Check current low-cost stays on our deals page, compare a Las Vegas or Orlando option to what your points would cost, and use the under $100 filter to find your own $99 win. Run the point math once, and you may never burn points on a cheap room again.
